summary: Specifies enhancements that let IP datagrams be routed to mobile nodes. A node keeps its home address while away, registers a care-of address with its home agent, and the home agent tunnels datagrams to it. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3344.

plainLanguage.summary: In IPv4 an address belongs to a place, so a laptop that moves to another network cannot keep the same address without help. Mobile IP adds that help: a router at home keeps track of where the laptop is and forwards traffic down a tunnel to it, so the laptop's address never changes.

subtitle: How an IPv4 host keeps its address while it moves, using a home agent, a tunnel and a registration.

tldr.problem: An IPv4 address identifies a place on the network, so a host that moves normally has to change its address or force host-specific routes through the whole Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The host keeps its home address and registers a care-of address with a home agent, which intercepts traffic for that address and tunnels it to the host.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3344, and it revises the original Mobile IP specifications with clarified rules and better security.

today: RFC 5944 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2010 that obsoletes RFC 3344, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its appendix lists what changed since RFC 3344 and the earlier Mobile IP specifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IP version 4 assumes that a node's IP address uniquely identifies the node's point of attachment to the Internet. A node must therefore be located on the network indicated by its IP address in order to receive datagrams destined to it. For a node to change its point of attachment without losing its ability to communicate, one of two mechanisms must typically be employed: the node must change its IP address whenever it changes its point of attachment, or host-specific routes must be propagated throughout much of the Internet routing fabric.

Both alternatives are often unacceptable. The first makes it impossible for a node to maintain transport and higher-layer connections when the node changes location. The second has obvious and severe scaling problems, especially relevant given the explosive growth in sales of notebook computers. A new, scalable mechanism is required for accommodating node mobility within the Internet, and this document defines such a mechanism, which enables nodes to change their point of attachment without changing their IP address.

The protocol requirements are that a mobile node must be able to communicate with other nodes after changing its link-layer point of attachment, without changing its IP address, and that it must be able to communicate with nodes that do not implement these mobility functions. No protocol enhancements are required in hosts or routers that are not acting as any of the new architectural entities. All messages used to update another node as to the location of a mobile node must be authenticated in order to protect against remote redirection attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that an address in IPv4 means a location. The RFC solves it by separating the address a host is known by from the place it is plugged in.

sections.title: New Architectural Entities
sections.content:
Mobile IP introduces three new functional entities. A mobile node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment from one network or subnetwork to another. It may change its location without changing its IP address and may continue to communicate with other Internet nodes at any location using that address, assuming link-layer connectivity to a point of attachment is available.

A home agent is a router on a mobile node's home network that tunnels datagrams for delivery to the mobile node when it is away from home, and maintains current location information for the mobile node. A foreign agent is a router on a mobile node's visited network that provides routing services to the mobile node while registered. The foreign agent detunnels and delivers to the mobile node datagrams that were tunnelled by the home agent, and for datagrams sent by a mobile node it may serve as a default router for registered mobile nodes.

A mobile node is given a long-term IP address on a home network, administered in the same way that a permanent address is provided to a stationary host. When away from its home network, a care-of address is associated with the mobile node and reflects its current point of attachment. The mobile node uses its home address as the source address of all IP datagrams it sends, except for the datagrams it sends for certain mobility management functions.

There are two ways to get a care-of address. A foreign agent care-of address is an address of a foreign agent, given in its Agent Advertisements. In that case the foreign agent is the endpoint of the tunnel and decapsulates the datagrams it receives, delivering the inner datagram to the mobile node. This mode is preferred because it lets many mobile nodes share one care-of address and so does not place unnecessary demands on the already limited IPv4 address space. A co-located care-of address is acquired by the mobile node as a local IP address through some external means, such as DHCP, and associated with one of its own interfaces. In that case the mobile node is the endpoint of the tunnel and performs the decapsulation itself. That mode lets a mobile node work without a foreign agent, but it does place additional burden on the IPv4 address space.
sections.plainLanguage: Three roles. The mobile node is the travelling host. The home agent is the router that owns its address and knows where it went. The foreign agent is the router in the visited network that stands in for it. The care-of address is the address traffic is actually sent to while the host is away.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
Three support services are defined for Mobile IP. Agent discovery lets home agents and foreign agents advertise their availability on each link for which they provide service, and a newly arrived mobile node can send a solicitation on the link to learn whether any prospective agents are present. Registration lets the mobile node register its care-of address with its home agent when it is away from home, either directly or through a foreign agent that forwards the registration. Silently discard means the implementation discards the datagram without further processing and without indicating an error to the sender, while providing the capability of logging the error and recording the event in a statistics counter.

The steps of operation are as follows. Mobility agents advertise their presence with Agent Advertisement messages, and a mobile node may solicit one from locally attached mobility agents. The mobile node receives the advertisements and determines whether it is on its home network or a foreign network. When it detects that it is located on its home network it operates without mobility services; if it is returning home it deregisters with its home agent by exchanging a Registration Request and a Registration Reply with it.

When the mobile node detects that it has moved to a foreign network it obtains a care-of address there, either from a foreign agent's advertisements or by an external assignment mechanism such as DHCP. It then registers its new care-of address with its home agent by exchanging a Registration Request and a Registration Reply, possibly via a foreign agent. Datagrams sent to the mobile node's home address are intercepted by its home agent, tunnelled to the care-of address, received at the tunnel endpoint, and delivered to the mobile node. In the reverse direction, datagrams sent by the mobile node are generally delivered to their destination using standard IP routing, not necessarily passing through the home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Find an agent, get an address, tell your home agent about it, and then traffic follows a tunnel. Traffic going the other way does not travel that route.

sections.title: Agent Discovery
sections.content:
Agent Advertisements are transmitted by a mobility agent to advertise its services on a link, and mobile nodes use them to determine their current point of attachment. An Agent Advertisement is an ICMP Router Advertisement extended to carry a Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension and, optionally, a Prefix-Lengths Extension, a One-byte Padding Extension or other extensions that might be defined in the future.

The ICMP fields have specific meanings here. The Code field is interpreted as follows: 0 means the mobility agent handles common traffic, that is, it acts as a router for IP datagrams not necessarily related to mobile nodes, and 16 means the mobility agent does not route common traffic, although all foreign agents must at least forward to a default router any datagrams received from a registered mobile node. The Lifetime is the maximum length of time the advertisement is considered valid in the absence of further advertisements. The TTL for all Agent Advertisements must be set to 1, and the IP destination address of a multicast advertisement must be either the all-systems-on-this-link address or the limited broadcast address, because mobile nodes will not generally know the prefix of the foreign network.

If advertisements are sent periodically, the nominal interval should be no longer than one third of the advertisement lifetime, so that a mobile node can miss three successive advertisements before deleting the agent from its list of valid agents. The actual transmission time should be slightly randomized to avoid synchronization and collisions with other advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: When the host arrives somewhere new, routers there announce themselves. The announcements are ordinary router advertisements with an extra field bolted on, and they are sent rarely enough that a host can lose three in a row and still keep the router.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content:
Registration is the mechanism by which mobile nodes communicate their current reachability information to their home agent. It is how they request forwarding services when visiting a foreign network, inform their home agent of their current care-of address, renew a registration that is due to expire, and deregister when they return home. Registration messages exchange information between a mobile node, optionally a foreign agent, and the home agent, and create or modify a mobility binding at the home agent that associates the mobile node's home address with its care-of address for the specified lifetime.

There are two registration procedures. If a mobile node is registering a foreign agent care-of address it must register via that foreign agent. If it is using a co-located care-of address and receives an Agent Advertisement from a foreign agent on the link where it uses that address, it should register via that foreign agent, or another on the same link, if the R bit is set in the advertisement. Otherwise it must register directly with its home agent, as it must also do when it has returned to its home network.

Registering via a foreign agent takes four messages: the mobile node sends a Registration Request to the prospective foreign agent; the foreign agent processes the request and relays it to the home agent; the home agent sends a Registration Reply to the foreign agent to grant or deny the request; and the foreign agent relays the reply to the mobile node. Registering directly with the home agent takes only two messages, the request and the reply.

The registration messages use UDP, with destination port 434. A nonzero UDP checksum should be included in the header and must be checked by the recipient, and a zero checksum should be accepted. Whether the two ends accept packets with a zero checksum should be defined as part of the Mobility Security Association between them. Registration messages between a mobile node and its home agent must be authenticated with an authorization-enabling extension, and that extension must be the first authentication extension in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering tells the home agent where you are and for how long. Through a foreign agent it takes four messages; directly it takes two. Either way the request is signed.

sections.title: The Registration Request Message
sections.content:
The Registration Request carries a type byte, a set of flag bits, a lifetime, the home address, the home agent address, the care-of address, a 64-bit identification number and a list of extensions. The type is 1 for a registration request. The S bit asks the home agent to retain prior mobility bindings. The B bit asks for broadcast datagrams received on the home network to be tunnelled to the mobile node. The D bit says the mobile node will itself decapsulate datagrams sent to the care-of address, that is, it is using a co-located care-of address. The M bit requests minimal encapsulation and the G bit requests GRE encapsulation. The r and x bits are sent as zero and ignored on receipt. The T bit requests reverse tunnelling.

The lifetime is the number of seconds remaining before the registration is considered expired. A value of zero indicates a request for deregistration, and a value of 0xffff indicates infinity. The identification number is a 64-bit value constructed by the mobile node, used for matching registration requests with replies and for protecting against replay attacks. The fixed portion of the message is followed by one or more extensions, and an authorization-enabling extension must be included in all registration requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a compact message with a handful of one-bit switches and the three addresses that matter: home, home agent and care-of. The lifetime field doubles as the deregister signal, with zero meaning please forget me.

sections.title: Datagram Routing with a Home Agent
sections.content:
The home agent must be able to intercept any datagrams on the home network addressed to the mobile node while the mobile node is registered away from home. Proxy and gratuitous ARP may be used to enable this interception. The home agent examines the IP destination address of all arriving datagrams to see whether it equals the home address of any of its mobile nodes registered away from home, and if so tunnels the datagram to the mobile node's currently registered care-of address or addresses. If the home agent supports multiple simultaneous mobility bindings it tunnels a copy to each care-of address in the binding list. If the mobile node has no current mobility bindings the home agent must not attempt to intercept datagrams destined for it, and if the home agent is also a router handling common traffic it will in general receive such datagrams for forwarding, in which case it must assume the mobile node is at home and forward the datagram directly onto the home network.

For multihomed home agents, the source address in the outer IP header of the encapsulated datagram must be the address sent to the mobile node in the Home Agent field of the Registration Reply. Nodes implementing tunnelling should also implement the tunnel soft state mechanism, which allows ICMP error messages returned from the tunnel to be reflected back to the original senders of the tunnelled datagrams.

If the lifetime for a given mobility binding expires before the home agent has received another valid registration request, the binding is deleted, and the home agent must not send a registration reply simply because the binding expired. When a mobility binding's lifetime expires the home agent must delete it, but it must retain any other, unexpired, simultaneous mobility bindings it holds for the mobile node.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent watches for traffic addressed to its mobile nodes and forwards each one down the tunnel. When the registration runs out, the entry is quietly removed and the traffic stops being intercepted.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mobile computing environment is potentially very different from the ordinary one. In many cases mobile computers are connected to the network via wireless links, which are particularly vulnerable to passive eavesdropping, active replay attacks and other active attacks.

Home agents and mobile nodes must be able to perform authentication. The default algorithm is HMAC-MD5 with a key size of 128 bits, and the foreign agent must also support HMAC-MD5 with key sizes of 128 bits or greater and manual key distribution, with keys of arbitrary binary values supported. The prefix-and-suffix use of MD5 to protect data and a shared secret is considered vulnerable to attack, so where backward compatibility with existing implementations is needed, new implementations should include keyed MD5 as an additional algorithm. The strength of the mechanism depends on the algorithm, the secrecy and strength of the key, and the quality of the implementation, and the 128-bit key must be both secret and pseudo-random.

The registration protocol results in a mobile node's traffic being tunnelled to its care-of address, and this could be a significant vulnerability if the registration were not authenticated. Remote redirection, for instance as performed by the mobile registration protocol, is widely understood to be a security problem in the current Internet if not authenticated. The Address Resolution Protocol is not authenticated and can potentially be used to steal another host's traffic, and the use of gratuitous ARP brings with it all of the risks associated with the use of ARP.

Because key distribution is difficult in the absence of a network key management protocol, messages with the foreign agent are not all required to be authenticated. In a commercial environment it might be important to authenticate all messages between the foreign agent and the home agent, so that billing is possible and service providers do not provide service to users who are not legitimate customers.

The identification field lets the home agent verify that a registration message has been freshly generated by the mobile node rather than replayed. Two methods are described: timestamps, which all mobile nodes and home agents must implement, and nonces, which they may implement. With timestamp-based protection the generator inserts the current time of day and the receiver checks that it is sufficiently close to its own. Unless the security association says otherwise, a default value of 7 seconds may be used to limit the time difference, and that value should be greater than 3 seconds. The 64-bit identification used in a registration request must be greater than that used in any previous request, because the home agent uses the value as a sequence number; without one, a delayed duplicate could arrive and be applied out of order, mistakenly altering the registered care-of address.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration is the dangerous part, because a forged one could redirect someone's traffic. The RFC signs every registration with a keyed hash and stamps it with a time so that an old copy cannot be replayed.

items.title: Mobile node
items.text: The host or router that moves between networks while keeping its IP address.

items.title: Home agent
items.text: A router on the home network that keeps track of the mobile node and tunnels its traffic to it.

items.title: Foreign agent
items.text: A router on the visited network that provides service to the mobile node while it is registered there.

items.title: Home address
items.text: The long-term address of the mobile node. It does not change when the node moves.

items.title: Care-of address
items.text: The address that reflects the mobile node's current point of attachment, and the end of the tunnel.

items.title: Mobility binding
items.text: The association of a home address with a care-of address, together with the remaining lifetime of that association.
